question: Does homeowners insurance cover earthquake damage in California?
aliases: Do I need separate earthquake insurance in California?
Is earthquake damage covered by my California homeowners policy?
Why is earthquake excluded from my California home insurance?
Does my home insurance pay if an earthquake damages my house in CA?
shortAnswer: Generally no, and California law says so in the statute itself: section 10083(a) prescribes the wording insurers must use for the mandatory earthquake offer, in at least 10-point boldface type, and that prescribed text begins 'Your residential property insurance policy does not cover earthquake damage to your home or its contents' [S:ca-ins-code-10083]. The California Department of Insurance tells consumers the same thing: 'Your homeowner's insurance does not cover earthquake damage' [S:cdi-earthquake-guide-925]. In filed forms this normally works as an exclusion rather than as silence; the California FAIR Plan's dwelling property form CFP 00 01 (05/2026) excludes 'Earth Movement, meaning earthquake,' with an ensuing-loss carve-out for fire and explosion, but that is one published form and wording varies, so the exclusion that governs is the one in your own form [S:cfp-dwelling-property-policy-form]. CDI states that California law requires both homeowners and renter's insurance to cover fire damage caused by or following an earthquake, whether or not you bought earthquake insurance [S:cdi-earthquake-guide-925]. To reach shake damage you need an earthquake endorsement or a separate earthquake policy, which section 10081 requires be offered to the named insured as a condition of issuing or delivering a residential property policy, and, for policies already in effect when chapter 8.5 took effect, on initial renewal [S:ca-ins-code-10081]. The offer does not have to come first: section 10083(a) allows it to be made 'prior to, concurrent with, or within 60 days following the issuance or renewal of a residential property insurance policy,' and section 10083(b) adds an every-other-year re-offer if you do not accept [S:ca-ins-code-10083]. CDI says most of that coverage in California comes from the California Earthquake Authority, a state-created entity, sold only through participating insurers [S:cdi-earthquake-guide-925][S:ca-ins-code-10089-point-6].
assumes: You are asking how California residential property forms and California statute are written, not how a specific claim on a specific policy should be decided. Coverage on a real claim is decided by the insurer under the actual policy, and disputes over it are legal questions.
The damage in question is physical damage from ground shaking, not fire, flood, tsunami, or a pre-existing condition.
No earthquake endorsement and no separate earthquake policy is already in force, unless stated otherwise.

The only two policy forms quoted here are the California FAIR Plan dwelling property form CFP 00 01 (05/2026) and CEA form BEQ-3B (01-2026 edition). Neither is a private carrier's filed homeowners form, and your own policy may read differently.
The statutes and forms cited are the versions published as of 2026-08-31. California statute and filed forms both change over time.
why:
The mechanism is an exclusion, not silence. The California FAIR Plan's published Dwelling Property Policy, form CFP 00 01 (05/2026), which states that it includes copyrighted material of Insurance Services Office, Inc. with its permission, excludes 'Earth Movement, meaning earthquake, including land shock waves or tremors before, during or after a volcanic eruption; landslide; mine subsidence; mudflow; earth sinking, rising or shifting; unless direct loss by: a. fire; or b. explosion; ensues and then we will pay only for the ensuing loss' [S:cfp-dwelling-property-policy-form]. Read that as one example of how the exclusion is drafted, not as the wording of every California residential policy: it is a single FAIR Plan form, and it is a dwelling fire form rather than a homeowners form [S:cfp-dwelling-property-policy-form]. Many forms use similar language, and only the wording in your own form governs your policy. What is not form-specific is the Legislature's own characterization of the market. The offer notice that section 10083(a) requires insurers to deliver, in at least 10-point boldface type, opens with the sentence 'Your residential property insurance policy does not cover earthquake damage to your home or its contents' [S:ca-ins-code-10083]. CDI states the same thing in consumer terms and adds that homeowners, renters, and condominium policies generally do not cover damage from natural disasters such as earthquakes, floods, and landslides [S:cdi-earthquake-guide-925].

Fire following an earthquake runs the other direction. The FAIR Plan earth movement exclusion quoted above ends with an ensuing-loss carve-out: if direct loss by fire or explosion ensues, the insurer pays for the ensuing loss [S:cfp-dwelling-property-policy-form]. CDI puts it as a legal requirement: 'California law says that both homeowners and renter's insurance must cover fire damage that is caused by or follows an earthquake,' and fire damage is therefore covered whether or not you have earthquake insurance [S:cdi-earthquake-guide-925]. The CEA homeowners form is the mirror image, and its LOSSES EXCLUDED section excludes loss caused directly or indirectly by 'Fire or explosion' [S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form]. CDI also lists fire among common earthquake insurance exclusions, in a list it presents as examples rather than a complete one [S:cdi-earthquake-guide-925]. Which policy responds to a particular post-quake fire, and how each policy's deductible applies, depends on those two policies' actual terms and on how the cause of loss is determined on the facts. The insurers make that determination in the first instance, and a policyholder who disagrees can take it up with CDI or a lawyer.

The offer of earthquake coverage is mandatory in California; the coverage is not. Section 10081 provides that no policy of residential property insurance may be issued or delivered in this state, or, with respect to policies in effect on the effective date of chapter 8.5, initially renewed, unless the named insured is offered coverage for loss or damage caused by the peril of earthquake, and that the coverage may sit in the residential policy itself by specific provision or endorsement or in a separate policy or certificate [S:ca-ins-code-10081]. The 'initially renewed' clause is limited by its own terms to policies that were already in force when the chapter took effect; section 10081 does not itself attach an offer duty to every renewal [S:ca-ins-code-10081]. The recurring duty comes from section 10083(b), which provides that if the offer is not accepted, the insurer or any affiliated insurer must, 'on an every other year basis,' offer earthquake coverage in connection with any continuation, renewal, or reinstatement of the policy following any lapse, or with respect to any other policy that extends, changes, supersedes, or replaces the residential policy [S:ca-ins-code-10083]. Section 10083(a) allows the offer to be made 'prior to, concurrent with, or within 60 days following the issuance or renewal of a residential property insurance policy' [S:ca-ins-code-10083]. Section 10083(a) also prescribes the text of the offer, with fill-in items for the dwelling or building coverage limit, the deductible, the contents coverage limit, the additional living expenses coverage limit, and the estimated annual premium, and with the sentence 'If you do not accept the offer of earthquake insurance below within 30 days of the mailing of this notice, your insurance company shall presume that you have not accepted this offer of earthquake insurance' [S:ca-ins-code-10083]. CDI describes the same mechanics for consumers: the offer must be in writing, must tell you the limits, the deductible, and the premium, and you have 30 days running from the date the company mails it, with no reply treated as a rejection [S:cdi-earthquake-guide-925].

What the mandatory offer must contain is set by statute and is deliberately modest. Section 10082(a) ties the offer to the minimum coverages in subdivisions (a) and (b) of section 10089 [S:ca-ins-code-10082]. Section 10089(a)(1) requires dwelling coverage and then lists what that coverage need not include: outbuildings, appurtenant structures, swimming pools, masonry fences and walls not necessary for the structural integrity of the dwelling, walkways and patios not necessary for regular ingress or egress from the dwelling, awnings or other patio coverings, decorative or artistic features including plaster if other covering would be more cost-effective, landscaping, and masonry chimneys, with the proviso that the policy covers replacement of a damaged masonry chimney with a nonmasonry, earthquake resistant chimney [S:ca-ins-code-10089]. Section 10089(a)(2) requires contents coverage of either not less than 10 percent of the amount of the covered dwelling loss or not less than $5,000, with the insurer electing which option at the time it files its rate application and then offering that option to every policyholder who receives an offer, and section 10089(a)(3) requires additional living expenses of no less than $1,500 while the residential dwelling remains uninhabitable due to physical loss or damage from the peril of earthquake [S:ca-ins-code-10089]. The 15 percent deductible cap sits in a separate subdivision, 10089(b), which provides that the dwelling and contents coverages shall not contain a deductible of more than 15 percent of coverage provided for the dwelling [S:ca-ins-code-10089]. A mandatory offer is not a promise that you can buy a policy: section 10082(b) provides that nothing in the chapter requires an insurer to issue a residential property policy except in accordance with the insurer's usual underwriting standards, while also providing that those standards shall not permit an insurer to provide a residential property policy unless the required offer is made [S:ca-ins-code-10082].

The California Earthquake Authority exists by statute. Section 10089.6(a)(1) creates the California Earthquake Authority and provides that it is administered and governed by the governing board described in section 10089.7 under the authority of the commissioner, with a further clause about oversight by the California Catastrophe Response Council limited to Wildfire Fund support services; the section sits in chapter 8.6 of the Insurance Code, added by Stats. 1995, Ch. 944, Sec. 2 [S:ca-ins-code-10089-point-6]. CEA's own account is that the Legislature created it in 1996 after the January 17, 1994 Northridge earthquake, that it is 'a not-for-profit, publicly managed, privately funded entity,' and that it 'provides two-thirds of the residential earthquake insurance policies sold in California'; that market-share figure is CEA's undated self-description with no stated methodology or as-of date [S:cea-history]. The CEA homeowners form describes CEA as a public instrumentality of the State of California established and authorized by law to transact insurance in California [S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form]. CDI states that you cannot purchase earthquake insurance directly from CEA, that it is sold by member companies known as Participating Insurers, and that you must purchase the CEA policy from the same insurance company that writes your residential property policy [S:cdi-earthquake-guide-925]. Form BEQ-3B (01-2026 edition) turns that link into a policy condition: the insured must keep a companion fire policy on the same property in force from the same participating insurer for the entire CEA policy period, and 'if no companion policy is in effect at the time of loss, this CEA policy is void and no payment will be made under this CEA policy' [S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form]. The California FAIR Plan says the same structure applies on its side: it offers earthquake coverage through CEA as a separate policy for customers with a FAIR Plan dwelling fire policy, and 'A stand-alone earthquake policy written by the California FAIR Plan is not available' [S:cfp-earthquake-page].

On the CEA homeowners form, shake, fire, water, and land are separate buckets. Form BEQ-3B (01-2026 edition) defines 'Earthquake' as a vibration-generating rupture event caused by displacement within the earth's crust through release of strain associated with tectonic processes, including effects such as ground shaking, liquefaction, and damaging amplification of ground motion, and closes the definition with 'Earthquake does not mean or include tsunami or volcanic eruption' [S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form]. Its LOSSES EXCLUDED section excludes water damage including flood, precipitation, surface water, 'waves, tsunami, or tidal water,' rupture of a dam, levee, berm, or sea wall, overflow of a natural or man-made body of water, and water below the surface of the ground, subject to narrow write-backs for earthquake-caused releases from water heaters, refrigerators, or water supply pipes within the dwelling, displacement of water from an aquarium, drinking water container or dispenser, swimming pool, decorative pool, spa, or hot tub, releases from municipal or other water supply lines or from sewers or drains, and precipitation entering through an opening in a roof or wall created by earthquake damage [S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form]. Land, including land underlying the dwelling, is listed as property not covered under Coverages A and B, along with land stabilization costs, except as provided under the OTHER COVERAGES item 3 'Land' benefit, which pays up to $10,000 as a sublimit of the combined Coverage A and B limit [S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form]. Earth movement, settling of land, land sliding, subsidence, mudflows, and earth sinking, rising or shifting are excluded unless the movement was induced by, and would not have occurred in the absence of, an earthquake commencing during the policy period and causes loss that manifests within one year after that earthquake [S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form]. Neither of the two forms quoted in this answer is written to respond to inundation: the CEA form excludes flood, waves, tsunami, and tidal water, and the FAIR Plan dwelling form excludes 'flood, surface water, waves, tidal water, overflow of a body of water, or spray from any of these' [S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form][S:cfp-dwelling-property-policy-form]. CDI lists flood among common earthquake insurance exclusions [S:cdi-earthquake-guide-925]. Whether a particular water loss falls inside or outside a given form is a determination for the insurer on the facts of the claim.

The deductible on the CEA homeowners form is a percentage, not a flat dollar amount. Form BEQ-3B (01-2026 edition) provides that the deductible percentage and the deductible amount in dollars are shown on the declarations page and that the deductible amount is a percentage of the combined single limit of insurance for Coverage A Dwelling and Coverage B Extensions to Dwelling, not of a dwelling limit alone [S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form]. Coverage D Loss of Use is not subject to a deductible, nor is the first $1,500 of Emergency Repairs coverage, and the deductible amount does not reduce any limit of insurance stated on the declarations [S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form]. CEA publishes the homeowners deductible choices as 5, 10, 15, 20, or 25 percent of the Coverage A and B limit, and states that the 5 percent and 10 percent options are not available for homes with a Coverage A dwelling limit greater than $1,000,000, or for dwellings of frame construction built before 1980 that are not on a slab foundation and do not have a verified retrofit [S:cea-homeowners-coverages-deductibles]. The form also states that it has no guaranteed replacement cost or extended replacement cost feature, and that its combined single limit is not modified by any such feature in the companion homeowners policy [S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form].
whatChanges: Whether an earthquake endorsement or a separate earthquake policy was actually in force on the date of loss. Section 10081 requires only that the coverage be offered, and it may sit in the residential policy by provision or endorsement or in a separate policy or certificate [S:ca-ins-code-10081].

Which peril the insurer determines caused the damage: shake, ensuing fire, water or tsunami, or earth movement. The two forms quoted here route each of those to a different clause [S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form][S:cfp-dwelling-property-policy-form].

Whether your residential insurer is a CEA participating insurer. CDI states that a CEA policy must be bought from the same company that writes your residential property policy [S:cdi-earthquake-guide-925].

Whether the companion fire policy from the same participating insurer stayed in force. Form BEQ-3B (01-2026 edition) states that if no companion policy is in effect at the time of loss, the CEA policy is void and no payment will be made under it [S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form].
Whether you accepted or declined the offer, which is what triggers the every-other-year re-offer duty in section 10083(b) [S:ca-ins-code-10083].
Timing on seismically induced earth movement. Form BEQ-3B (01-2026 edition) requires the loss to manifest within one year after the earthquake that caused it [S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form].
variability: This answer is California-specific. The mandatory offer, the 60-day offer window, and the every-other-year re-offer duty come from California Insurance Code chapter 8.5 and do not apply outside California [S:ca-ins-code-10081][S:ca-ins-code-10083].

Form language varies, and only two published California forms are quoted here: the FAIR Plan dwelling property form CFP 00 01 (05/2026) and CEA form BEQ-3B (01-2026 edition). Neither is a private carrier's filed homeowners form, so an exclusion in one form should not be read as universal [S:cfp-dwelling-property-policy-form][S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form].

Both forms quoted here were refiled in 2026, and both publishers revise forms periodically. Re-pull the quoted language from the then-current edition before relying on it [S:cfp-dwelling-property-policy-form][S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form].

Availability is an underwriting question, not a statutory one. Section 10082(b) provides that nothing in the chapter requires an insurer to issue a residential property policy except in accordance with the insurer's usual underwriting standards [S:ca-ins-code-10082].

By CEA's own undated account it writes two-thirds of the residential earthquake policies sold in California, so earthquake coverage written by a non-CEA insurer can carry limits, deductibles, and exclusions different from the CEA form described here [S:cea-history][S:cdi-earthquake-guide-925].
nextActions: Pull your declarations page and look for an earthquake endorsement or a separate earthquake policy number, then ask your insurer or agent in writing to confirm what is in force. Do not settle the question from the declarations page alone.

Ask your insurer or agent for the earthquake offer. Section 10083(a) prescribes its language and gives it fill-in items for the dwelling or building limit, the deductible, the contents limit, the additional living expenses limit, and the estimated annual premium, and CDI says the offer must be in writing and that the 30-day period runs from the mailing date [S:ca-ins-code-10083][S:cdi-earthquake-guide-925].

Read the LOSSES EXCLUDED section of any earthquake policy you are offered before you buy it, and check specifically how it treats fire, water and tsunami, land, and seismically induced earth movement [S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form].

Model the deductible before deciding. On the CEA homeowners form the deductible is a percentage of the combined single limit for Coverage A and Coverage B shown on the declarations, and CEA publishes options of 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 percent with the two lowest restricted by dwelling limit and construction [S:cea-beq3b-homeowners-policy-form][S:cea-homeowners-coverages-deductibles]. CDI directs consumers to CEA's premium calculator [S:cdi-earthquake-guide-925].

If you already have damage, notify your residential insurer and any earthquake insurer and let each decide coverage under its own policy. CDI gives its Consumer Assistance Hotline as 1-800-927-4357 and says you may file a Request for Assistance against an insurer or an agent or broker by mail or online [S:cdi-earthquake-guide-925].
author: Aaron Bollinger

handoff.reason: The general rule is settled, but the decisions that follow it are not. Choosing a deductible percentage, deciding between a CEA policy and a non-CEA earthquake policy, and confirming whether a specific insurer is a CEA participating insurer all turn on filed forms, current rate filings, and that insurer's own underwriting, none of which a general research page can determine. A licensed agent or broker can request the statutory offer, read the specific form, and confirm terms. On a live claim, whether a loss is covered is a determination for the insurer under the actual policy, and a dispute about it is a legal question for a lawyer rather than something to settle from a general description of form language.
